title: The history of comets
tagline: From omens on clay tablets and palm-leaf texts to a spacecraft landing on a comet and visitors from other stars.
intro: For thousands of years comets were sudden, frightening visitors, recorded by astronomers in China, Babylon, India and Europe as signs of change. Tycho showed they fly far beyond the Moon, Newton put them on orbits and Halley predicted one would return. In the twentieth century scientists worked out what comets are made of and where they come from, and since 1986 spacecraft have flown past, crashed into and landed on them.

eras.name: Omens and records
eras.summary: Comets are signs in the sky, recorded with great care in China, Babylon, India and Europe.

eras.name: Travellers among the planets
eras.summary: Tycho puts a comet beyond the Moon, Newton gives comets orbits, and Halley's comet comes back on time.

eras.name: What comets are
eras.summary: Spectra, the dirty snowball, the Oort cloud, the Kuiper belt and a wind from the Sun.

eras.name: Visiting comets
eras.summary: Spacecraft fly past, crash into, collect dust from and finally land on comets.

eras.name: Strangers and sky surveys
eras.summary: Survey telescopes find interstellar visitors, and a spacecraft nudges an asteroid.

events.title: China records Halley's comet
events.who: Court astronomers of the Qin state
events.text: The Shiji, a history of China, records a 'broom star' in 240 BCE. It is the earliest sighting that can be matched with certainty to Halley's comet.
events.why: Old records like this let modern astronomers trace Halley's orbit back over two thousand years.

events.title: Babylonian clay tablets
events.text: Astronomers in Babylon pressed notes about Halley's comet into clay tablets in 164 BCE and again in 87 BCE.
events.why: They kept careful night-by-night diaries of the sky, and some survive.

events.title: A chapter on comets in the Bṛhat Saṃhitā
events.text: Varāhamihira's great Sanskrit encyclopaedia has a chapter on ketus, which include comets, and on what people thought they foretold. Sanskrit calls a comet a dhūmaketu, a smoky banner.
events.why: It shows Indian sky-watchers sorting and recording comets as carefully as any culture of the time.

events.title: A comet on the Bayeux Tapestry
events.text: The Bayeux Tapestry, made after the Norman conquest of England, shows people pointing at Halley's comet of 1066, which was seen as an omen.
events.why: It is one of the most famous pictures of a comet ever made.

events.title: Giotto paints a comet as the Star of Bethlehem
events.text: In his Adoration of the Magi, Giotto painted the star as a blazing comet. It is traditionally linked to Halley's return of 1301, though some historians now argue another comet was the model.
events.why: Centuries later, ESA named its comet probe Giotto.

events.title: Tycho puts a comet beyond the Moon
events.text: Tycho measured the Great Comet of 1577 from his island observatory and found it shifted against the stars far less than the Moon does. So it had to be much farther away.
events.why: It proved comets are not weather in our air but travellers among the planets.

events.title: Jahangir records two comets
events.text: The Mughal emperor Jahangir described two comets seen in November 1618 in his memoirs, the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri. A 2016 study argues he spotted them independently of European observers.
events.why: It is a careful Indian record from the year astronomers worldwide were watching the same comets.

events.title: Newton puts a comet on an orbit
events.text: In his Principia Newton showed that the Great Comet of 1680 moved on a long curve round the Sun under the same gravity that holds the planets.
events.why: Comets became part of physics: their paths could be calculated.

events.title: Halley predicts a return
events.text: In his Synopsis of the Astronomy of Comets, Halley argued that the comets of 1531, 1607 and 1682 were one object on a long ellipse, and predicted it would return in 1758.
events.why: It was the first prediction that a comet would come back.

events.title: The comet comes back
events.who: Johann Georg Palitzsch; Alexis Clairaut, Jérôme Lalande and Nicole-Reine Lepaute
events.text: A farmer and amateur astronomer, Palitzsch, spotted the returning comet on Christmas night 1758. In Paris, Clairaut, Lalande and Lepaute had worked out how Jupiter and Saturn would delay it; it passed the Sun on 13 March 1759.
events.why: Newton's gravity had predicted a comet's return, and it bears Halley's name ever since.

events.title: A comet seen from Madras
events.text: Searching for the lost comet Biela, Pogson at Madras found a comet-like object on two nights. With too few sightings for an orbit it is listed as X/1872 X1, probably not Biela.
events.why: It is an early comet find from an Indian observatory, and a reminder that not every sighting can be pinned down.

events.title: Earth passes through Halley's tail
events.text: Spectra had shown cyanogen gas in comet tails, and when the Earth passed through Halley's tail some people panicked and bought 'comet pills'. Nothing happened: the tail is far too thin to harm anyone.
events.why: It is a lesson in how a scientific fact can be turned into a scare.

events.title: The dirty snowball
events.text: Whipple proposed that a comet's heart is a solid 'icy conglomerate' of ices and dust. Jets of gas from the warmed side would push the comet like a weak rocket, explaining why some arrived early or late.
events.why: It is the model every space mission since has tested and refined.

events.title: A cloud of comets far away
events.text: Oort noticed that many long-period comets fall in from about the same huge distance, from every direction. He argued that a vast, round cloud of comets surrounds the Solar System.
events.why: No one has seen the Oort cloud directly, but it explains where long-period comets come from.

events.title: Comet tails reveal a wind from the Sun
events.text: Biermann saw that ion tails are pushed away from the Sun far harder than sunlight alone can manage. He argued that the Sun must blow out a constant stream of particles. Eugene Parker's theory of the solar wind followed in 1958.
events.why: Comets were the first solar-wind detectors.

events.title: A belt beyond Neptune
events.text: Edgeworth (1943, 1949) and Kuiper (1951) wrote about a band of small icy bodies past Neptune. The idea grew into the Kuiper belt, source of the short-period comets.
events.why: It pointed to a second store of comets, much closer than the Oort cloud.

events.title: The Halley armada
events.who: ESA, the Soviet Union and Japan
events.text: Five spacecraft flew past Halley's comet. The Soviet Vega probes and Japan's Suisei and Sakigake went first; ESA's Giotto then passed within about 600 km of the nucleus on 14 March and photographed it: about 15 km long, and so dark it reflected only 2 to 4% of the sunlight.
events.why: For the first time people saw a comet's nucleus, and it was black, not white.

events.title: The Kuiper belt is found
events.text: After five years of searching, Jewitt and Luu found 1992 QB1, a small icy world beyond Neptune: the first Kuiper belt object after Pluto and Charon.
events.why: The predicted belt was real; thousands more have been found since.

events.title: Comet pieces hit Jupiter
events.who: Carolyn and Eugene Shoemaker, David Levy
events.text: Comet Shoemaker–Levy 9, found in March 1993, had been torn into about 21 pieces when it passed close to Jupiter in July 1992. In July 1994 they crashed into Jupiter at about 60 km/s, leaving dark scars bigger than the Earth.
events.why: It was the first collision between two Solar System bodies ever watched.

events.title: Hale–Bopp, the comet everyone saw
events.text: Found on 23 July 1995, Hale–Bopp stayed visible to the naked eye for about 18 months, a record, with a nucleus perhaps 60 km across. It passed the Sun on 1 April 1997.
events.why: It was probably the most widely seen comet in history.

events.title: Deep Impact hits a comet
events.text: NASA's Deep Impact fired a copper impactor into comet Tempel 1 at about 10 km/s and studied the cloud of dust and ice it blasted out.
events.why: It showed what lies just under a comet's crust.

events.title: Comet dust comes to Earth
events.text: Stardust flew through comet Wild 2's coma on 2 January 2004, caught dust in a light foam called aerogel and landed it in Utah in 2006. In 2009 scientists found glycine, an amino acid, in the samples.
events.why: For the first time scientists could hold comet dust in the laboratory.

events.title: Rosetta arrives and Philae lands
events.who: ESA, with DLR and other partners
events.text: Launched in March 2004, ESA's Rosetta reached comet 67P on 6 August 2014 and released the lander Philae, which touched down on 12 November 2014: the first landing on a comet.
events.why: Rosetta then flew beside the comet for two years as it warmed and woke up.

events.title: Rosetta measures the comet's heavy water
events.text: Rosetta found that 67P's water has a deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio more than three times that of Earth's oceans. In 2024 a NASA-led reanalysis argued that dust had pushed the reading up.
events.why: It reopened the question of how much of Earth's water came from comets.

events.title: Ingredients for life, and a gentle end
events.text: Rosetta's instruments found glycine and phosphorus round 67P (announced in May 2016). On 30 September 2016 Rosetta was steered down onto the comet to end the mission.
events.why: Comets carry some of the chemistry life is built from.

events.title: A visitor from another star
events.text: A survey telescope found 'Oumuamua moving too fast to be bound to the Sun. The IAU created a new I/ class for it: 1I, the first known interstellar object. It showed no clear coma.
events.why: It proved that small bodies travel between the stars.

events.title: Borisov, an interstellar comet
events.text: An amateur astronomer with a home-made telescope found 2I/Borisov, the first clearly comet-like visitor from another star. Indian astronomers studied it with the Himalayan Chandra Telescope at Hanle and the 1.2 m telescope at Mount Abu and found it rich in CN gas.
events.why: Comets round other stars seem to be made of much the same stuff as ours.

events.title: NEOWISE lights up a lockdown sky
events.text: Found on 27 March 2020, comet NEOWISE reached about magnitude 1 in July and was seen by people all over the world.
events.why: It was the brightest comet in the northern sky since Hale–Bopp.

events.title: DART pushes an asteroid
events.where: Dimorphos, moon of the asteroid Didymos
events.text: NASA's DART spacecraft hit Dimorphos and shortened its orbit round Didymos from 11 h 55 min to 11 h 23 min.
events.why: The first test of moving a space rock on purpose. It was an asteroid, not a comet.

events.title: Tsuchinshan–ATLAS over India
events.who: Purple Mountain Observatory and the ATLAS survey
events.text: Comet C/2023 A3 passed the Sun on 27 September 2024 and shone in October evening skies, seen widely from India. In March 2024 the SOHO spacecraft had found its 5,000th comet, most of them sungrazers.
events.why: Bright comets are rare, and nobody can promise the next one.

events.title: A third interstellar visitor
events.text: 3I/ATLAS was found on 1 July 2025 and passed the Sun around 30 October 2025, about 1.4 AU out. In November 2025 India's Physical Research Laboratory observed it from Mount Abu and found its gases fairly typical of comets.
events.why: Three interstellar objects in eight years: survey telescopes are finding what was always passing through.

people.name: Varāhamihira
people.note: His Bṛhat Saṃhitā has a chapter on comets and other ketus.

people.name: Tycho Brahe
people.note: Measured the comet of 1577 and showed it was far beyond the Moon.

people.name: Edmond Halley
people.note: Predicted that the comet of 1682 would return in 1758.

people.name: Nicole-Reine Lepaute
people.note: Helped compute how Jupiter and Saturn would delay Halley's 1759 return.

people.name: Fred Whipple
people.note: Proposed the icy 'dirty snowball' nucleus in 1950.

people.name: Jan Oort
people.note: Argued in 1950 for a vast cloud of comets round the Solar System.

people.name: Carolyn Shoemaker
people.note: Co-discovered Shoemaker–Levy 9 and found more comets than almost anyone of her time.

people.name: Jane Luu
people.note: With David Jewitt, found the first Kuiper belt object after Pluto in 1992.

series.title: Comets found by the SOHO spacecraft
series.caption: Most of SOHO's finds are tiny sungrazers of the Kreutz family, spotted in its images by volunteers.

facts: A comet's nucleus is very dark: Giotto found Halley's reflects only 2 to 4% of the sunlight that hits it.
Comet 67P is so light for its size that a 50 kg person would weigh about as much as a gram does on Earth.
Comet Hyakutake's ion tail was crossed by the Ulysses probe at least 550 million km from the comet.
Comets' tails point away from the Sun, so a comet heading out into space travels tail-first.
The Perseid meteors every August are dust from comet Swift–Tuttle, hitting the air at about 59 km/s.
